items.stem: What is meant by effective demand?
options: The total quantity of a good that consumers would like to have
Demand at the equilibrium price only
The desire for a good backed by the ability and willingness to pay for it
The demand of consumers who are well informed
items.answer: The desire for a good backed by the ability and willingness to pay for it
items.markingKey: Effective demand = want + ability to pay.

items.stem: Explain the difference between demand and effective demand.
items.answer: Demand in economics is effective demand: the quantity consumers are willing and able to buy at each price in a time period. A desire for a good without the ability to pay is not effective demand.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: willing and able; 1 mark: desire alone not enough [2]

items.stem: Explain why a fall in the price of a good leads to an increase in the quantity demanded.
items.answer: The good becomes cheaper relative to substitutes, so consumers switch to it (substitution effect); real income rises so they can afford more (income effect); new consumers enter the market.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: substitution effect; 1 mark: income effect/new buyers [2]

items.stem: The table shows the weekly demand for gym memberships of the only three consumers in a market. Price ($): 2, 4, 6, 8; Consumer X (units): 20, 19, 18, 17; Consumer Y (units): 10, 8, 6, 4; Consumer Z (units): 20, 17, 14, 11. Calculate the market quantity demanded at a price of $8.
items.answer: 32 units

items.stem: The table shows the weekly demand for fresh fruit of the only three consumers in a market. Price ($): 2, 4, 6, 8; Consumer X (units): 12, 11, 10, 9; Consumer Y (units): 20, 18, 16, 14; Consumer Z (units): 10, 8, 6, 4. (a) Calculate the market demand at each price. (b) Calculate the percentage change in market quantity demanded when the price changes from $4 to $8. (c) Explain why the market demand curve slopes downwards.
items.answer: (a) 42, 37, 32, 27 units at $2, $4, $6, $8. (b) −27% (c) Each consumer buys more at lower prices (substitution and income effects), so the sum also rises as price falls.
items.markingKey: (a) horizontal summation [2] (b) (27 − 37)/37 × 100 [1] (c) law of demand reason [1] [4]

items.stem: Extract: The price of coffee beans on world markets rose from $2.0 to $2.6 per kilogram after frosts damaged crops in major producing countries. In Istrana, cafés raised the price of a cup of coffee, yet the number of cups sold in Riyadh still rose slightly because incomes grew by 5% and coffee became more fashionable among young people. Sales of tea fell. (a) Calculate the percentage increase in the world price of coffee beans. (b) Explain the effect of the frosts on the supply curve of coffee beans.
items.answer: (a) 30% (b) Shift to the left: fewer beans available at every price.
items.markingKey: (a) (2.6 − 2.0)/2.0 × 100 [2] (b) Credit: Shift to the left: fewer beans available at every price. [2]

items.stem: What does the law of demand state?
options: As price falls, quantity demanded rises, ceteris paribus
As price rises, demand rises for all goods
items.answer: As price falls, quantity demanded rises, ceteris paribus
items.markingKey: Inverse relationship between price and quantity demanded.

items.stem: Explain how a market demand curve is derived from individual demand curves.
items.answer: At each price the quantities demanded by every consumer in the market are added together (horizontal summation) to give total market demand.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: summation of quantities; 1 mark: at each price [2]

items.stem: The table shows the weekly demand for fresh fruit of the only three consumers in a market. Price ($): 2, 4, 6, 8; Consumer X (units): 15, 13, 11, 9; Consumer Y (units): 12, 9, 6, 3; Consumer Z (units): 12, 9, 6, 3. (a) Calculate the market demand at each price. (b) Calculate the percentage change in market quantity demanded when the price changes from $8 to $4. (c) Explain why the market demand curve slopes downwards.
items.answer: (a) 39, 31, 23, 15 units at $2, $4, $6, $8. (b) +106.7% (c) Each consumer buys more at lower prices (substitution and income effects), so the sum also rises as price falls.
items.markingKey: (a) horizontal summation [2] (b) (31 − 15)/15 × 100 [1] (c) law of demand reason [1] [4]

items.stem: Which causes a movement along the demand curve for a good?
options: A change in the price of a substitute
A change in the price of the good itself
items.answer: A change in the price of the good itself
items.markingKey: Own price → movement; other factors → shift.

items.stem: Explain the difference between a movement along a demand curve and a shift of a demand curve.
items.answer: A movement (extension or contraction) is caused only by a change in the good’s own price; a shift is caused by a change in any other condition of demand, such as income or tastes, changing the quantity demanded at every price.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: movement = own price; 1 mark: shift = other factors/at every price [2]

items.stem: Explain how an increase in income affects demand for normal and inferior goods.
items.answer: For a normal good demand rises (curve shifts right); for an inferior good demand falls (curve shifts left) as consumers switch to better alternatives.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: normal; 1 mark: inferior [2]

items.stem: Incomes fall in Tarvia and consumers regard bicycles as an inferior good. What is the effect on the demand curve for bicycles?
options: Shift of the demand curve to the right
Shift of the demand curve to the left
items.answer: Shift of the demand curve to the right
items.markingKey: Shift of the demand curve to the right: demand for inferior goods rises when income falls.

items.stem: The price of a complement to textbooks rises sharply. What is the effect on the demand curve for textbooks? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Shift of the demand curve to the left: goods are used together, so demand for textbooks falls at every price.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: Shift of the demand curve to the left; 1 mark: explanation – goods are used together, so demand for textbooks falls at every price. [2]

items.stem: For each change, state the effect on the demand curve for textbooks and explain why. (i) A successful advertising campaign for textbooks is launched. (ii) A widely reported health study warns about the harm caused by textbooks, changing tastes.
items.answer: (i) Shift of the demand curve to the right (ii) Shift of the demand curve to the left
items.markingKey: (i) Shift of the demand curve to the right – tastes/preferences shift in favour of the good. [2] (ii) Shift of the demand curve to the left – tastes and preferences have moved against the good. [2] Total [4]

items.stem: Extract: The price of coffee beans on world markets rose from $1.5 to $2.1 per kilogram after frosts damaged crops in major producing countries. In Pelora, cafés raised the price of a cup of coffee, yet the number of cups sold in Mumbai still rose slightly because incomes grew by 4% and coffee became more fashionable among young people. Sales of tea fell. (a) Calculate the percentage increase in the world price of coffee beans. (b) Explain why sales of tea fell.
items.answer: (a) 40% (b) Changes in tastes towards coffee shifted demand for tea (a substitute) to the left.
items.markingKey: (a) (2.1 − 1.5)/1.5 × 100 [2] (b) Credit: Changes in tastes towards coffee shifted demand for tea (a substitute) to the left. [2]

items.stem: Extract: The price of coffee beans on world markets rose from $2.0 to $2.6 per kilogram after frosts damaged crops in major producing countries. In Lunaria, cafés raised the price of a cup of coffee, yet the number of cups sold in Mexico City still rose slightly because incomes grew by 4% and coffee became more fashionable among young people. Sales of tea fell. (a) Explain the effect of the frosts on the supply curve of coffee beans. (b) Explain why sales of cups of coffee rose despite the higher price.
items.answer: (a) Shift to the left: fewer beans available at every price. (b) Demand shifted right (higher incomes, fashion) by more than the contraction caused by the price rise.
items.markingKey: (a) Credit: Shift to the left: fewer beans available at every price. [2] (b) Credit: Demand shifted right (higher incomes, fashion) by more than the contraction caused by the price rise. [3]

items.stem: Which would shift the demand curve for coffee to the right?
options: A fall in the price of coffee
A rise in the price of tea
A rise in the price of sugar
A fall in consumers’ incomes, if coffee is normal
items.answer: A rise in the price of tea
items.markingKey: Tea is a substitute; demand for coffee rises at every price.

items.stem: Explain why expectations of a future price rise may shift the current demand curve.
items.answer: Consumers buy now before the price rises, so current demand rises at every price: the demand curve shifts right.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: buy now; 1 mark: shift right [2]

items.stem: A new train line makes it quicker to travel from Madrid to the coast. Explain the effect on the demand for car hire in Madrid.
items.answer: Rail travel is a substitute: demand for car hire falls at every price, shifting the demand curve to the left.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: substitute; 1 mark: shift left [2]

items.stem: The demand for rice in Umbria Nova is Qd = 200 − 10P. After a successful advertising campaign, demand becomes Qd = 220 − 10P. Calculate the change in quantity demanded at a price of $5.
items.answer: +20 units
items.markingKey: Before 150, after 170; change +20.

items.stem: Extract: The price of coffee beans on world markets rose from $2.0 to $2.6 per kilogram after frosts damaged crops in major producing countries. In Korvia, cafés raised the price of a cup of coffee, yet the number of cups sold in Lagos still rose slightly because incomes grew by 3% and coffee became more fashionable among young people. Sales of tea fell. (a) Calculate the percentage increase in the world price of coffee beans. (b) Explain why sales of tea fell.
items.answer: (a) 30% (b) Changes in tastes towards coffee shifted demand for tea (a substitute) to the left.
items.markingKey: (a) (2.6 − 2.0)/2.0 × 100 [2] (b) Credit: Changes in tastes towards coffee shifted demand for tea (a substitute) to the left. [2]

items.stem: What does the law of supply state?
options: As price rises, the quantity supplied rises, ceteris paribus
As price falls, quantity supplied rises
items.answer: As price rises, the quantity supplied rises, ceteris paribus
items.markingKey: Positive relationship: higher prices → more profitable → more supplied.

items.stem: Explain why a supply curve slopes upwards from left to right.
items.answer: At higher prices it is more profitable to produce, so existing firms expand output and new firms enter; higher prices also cover the rising marginal cost of extra output.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: profit incentive; 1 mark: rising costs/new firms [2]

items.stem: Explain two factors that could cause the supply curve for a good to shift to the left.
items.answer: Higher costs of production (wages, raw materials, energy); indirect taxes; adverse weather/natural disasters; fewer firms; removal of subsidies.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each factor explained [2]

items.stem: A flood destroys factories producing solar panels in Calvania. What is the effect on the supply curve of solar panels?
options: Shift of the supply curve to the left
Shift of the supply curve to the right
items.answer: Shift of the supply curve to the left
items.markingKey: Shift of the supply curve to the left: productive capacity falls.

items.stem: The government gives producers of bottled water a subsidy. What is the effect on the supply curve of bottled water? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Shift of the supply curve to the right: a subsidy lowers producers’ costs.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: Shift of the supply curve to the right; 1 mark: explanation – a subsidy lowers producers’ costs. [2]

items.stem: For each change, state the effect on the supply curve and explain why. (i) A flood destroys factories producing running shoes in Merania. (ii) A new technology reduces the cost of producing running shoes.
items.answer: (i) Shift of the supply curve to the left (ii) Shift of the supply curve to the right
items.markingKey: (i) Shift of the supply curve to the left – productive capacity falls. [2] (ii) Shift of the supply curve to the right – lower unit costs raise supply at every price. [2] Total [4]

items.stem: Extract: The price of coffee beans on world markets rose from $2.0 to $2.6 per kilogram after frosts damaged crops in major producing countries. In Tarvia, cafés raised the price of a cup of coffee, yet the number of cups sold in Cape Town still rose slightly because incomes grew by 5% and coffee became more fashionable among young people. Sales of tea fell. (a) Calculate the percentage increase in the world price of coffee beans. (b) Explain why sales of tea fell.
items.answer: (a) 30% (b) Changes in tastes towards coffee shifted demand for tea (a substitute) to the left.
items.markingKey: (a) (2.6 − 2.0)/2.0 × 100 [2] (b) Credit: Changes in tastes towards coffee shifted demand for tea (a substitute) to the left. [2]

items.stem: Extract: The price of coffee beans on world markets rose from $3.0 to $3.9 per kilogram after frosts damaged crops in major producing countries. In Esteria, cafés raised the price of a cup of coffee, yet the number of cups sold in Kuala Lumpur still rose slightly because incomes grew by 3% and coffee became more fashionable among young people. Sales of tea fell. (a) Calculate the percentage increase in the world price of coffee beans. (b) Explain why sales of cups of coffee rose despite the higher price.
items.answer: (a) 30% (b) Demand shifted right (higher incomes, fashion) by more than the contraction caused by the price rise.
items.markingKey: (a) (3.9 − 3.0)/3.0 × 100 [2] (b) Credit: Demand shifted right (higher incomes, fashion) by more than the contraction caused by the price rise. [3]

items.stem: Explain the difference between an increase in supply and an increase in quantity supplied.
items.answer: An increase in supply is a rightward shift caused by a non-price factor; an increase in quantity supplied is an extension along the curve caused by a rise in the good’s own price.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: Farmers in Marvona expect the price of their crop to rise next year. Explain why current supply may fall.
items.answer: Farmers hold back stocks to sell later at the higher price, so current supply shifts left.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: withhold stock; 1 mark: current supply falls [2]

items.stem: The supply of bottled water is given by Qs = −20 + 3P, where Q is in thousands of units and P in dollars. Calculate the quantity supplied when the price is $10.
items.answer: 10 thousand

items.stem: For each change, state the effect on the supply curve and explain why. (i) The price of cement falls. (ii) The government gives producers of cement a subsidy. (iii) The price of cement rises.
items.answer: (i) Movement along the supply curve (contraction) (ii) Shift of the supply curve to the right (iii) Movement along the supply curve (extension)
items.markingKey: (i) Movement along the supply curve (contraction) – own-price change: movement down the curve. [2] (ii) Shift of the supply curve to the right – a subsidy lowers producers’ costs. [2] (iii) Movement along the supply curve (extension) – own-price change: firms supply more at a higher price. [2] Total [6]

items.stem: Explain why the supply curve slopes upwards and the factors that can cause it to shift.
items.answer: Profit motive, rising marginal cost, entry of firms; shifts from costs, technology, taxes/subsidies, weather, number of firms, expectations; diagram.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Profit motive, rising marginal cost, entry of firms; shifts from costs, technology, taxes/subsidies, weather, number of firms, expectations; diagram. Level 3 (6–8): accurate knowledge with a clear, developed analytical chain and, where relevant, an accurate, labelled diagram that is used in the answer; Level 2 (3–5): some correct explanation but undeveloped or partly inaccurate; Level 1 (1–2): limited knowledge, mostly assertion [8]

items.stem: How is the market demand curve derived?
options: By adding the prices that each consumer would pay
By adding the quantities demanded by all individual consumers at each price
items.answer: By adding the quantities demanded by all individual consumers at each price
items.markingKey: Horizontal summation of individual demand curves.

items.stem: Cobalt Group cuts the price of chocolate bars by 10% and sales rise. Explain why, using the law of demand.
items.answer: Lower price raises quantity demanded: the product is cheaper relative to substitutes and consumers’ real income rises.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: inverse relationship; 1 mark: reason [2]

items.stem: Many people in Santiago would like to own an electric car, but sales remain low. Explain this using the concept of effective demand.
items.answer: Desire is not backed by ability to pay at current prices, so it is not effective demand; only those willing and able to buy count in the market.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: definition; 1 mark: application [2]

items.stem: The table shows the weekly demand for chocolate bars of the only three consumers in a market. Price ($): 2, 4, 6, 8; Consumer X (units): 12, 10, 8, 6; Consumer Y (units): 12, 11, 10, 9; Consumer Z (units): 10, 8, 6, 4. Calculate the market quantity demanded at a price of $4.
items.answer: 29 units

items.stem: Ethan, an economics student in Santiago, is preparing for a class debate on this topic. Explain the law of demand and how a market demand curve is derived.
items.answer: Effective demand; inverse P–Qd relationship; income and substitution effects; diminishing marginal utility; horizontal summation of individual demand curves; diagram.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Effective demand; inverse P–Qd relationship; income and substitution effects; diminishing marginal utility; horizontal summation of individual demand curves; diagram. Level 3 (6–8): accurate knowledge with a clear, developed analytical chain and, where relevant, an accurate, labelled diagram that is used in the answer; Level 2 (3–5): some correct explanation but undeveloped or partly inaccurate; Level 1 (1–2): limited knowledge, mostly assertion [8]

items.stem: Extract: The price of coffee beans on world markets rose from $3.0 to $3.9 per kilogram after frosts damaged crops in major producing countries. In Ostrelia, cafés raised the price of a cup of coffee, yet the number of cups sold in Doha still rose slightly because incomes grew by 5% and coffee became more fashionable among young people. Sales of tea fell. (a) Calculate the percentage increase in the world price of coffee beans. (b) Discuss whether the rise in coffee prices is likely to be permanent.
items.answer: (a) 30% (b) Supply recovers after frosts (new crops), new producers enter; but climate change may cause repeated shocks; demand growth persists; judgement.
items.markingKey: (a) (3.9 − 3.0)/3.0 × 100 [2] (b) Credit: Supply recovers after frosts (new crops), new producers enter; but climate change may cause repeated shocks; demand growth persists; judgement. [4]

items.stem: What is meant by the conditions of demand?
options: The time it takes to deliver goods
The factors other than the good’s own price that determine demand
The legal rules for selling goods
The prices at which firms are willing to supply
items.answer: The factors other than the good’s own price that determine demand
items.markingKey: Income, prices of related goods, tastes, population, advertising, expectations.

items.stem: The price of games consoles falls sharply in Esteria. Explain the effect on the demand for video games.
items.answer: Consoles and games are complements: more consoles are bought, so demand for games rises at every price (shift right).
items.markingKey: 1 mark: complements; 1 mark: shift right [2]

items.stem: The price of games consoles falls sharply in Ostrelia. Explain the effect on the demand for video games.
items.answer: Consoles and games are complements: more consoles are bought, so demand for games rises at every price (shift right).
items.markingKey: 1 mark: complements; 1 mark: shift right [2]

items.stem: The price of chocolate bars rises. What is the effect on the demand curve for chocolate bars?
options: Shift of the demand curve to the left
Shift of the demand curve to the right
items.answer: Movement along the demand curve (contraction)
items.markingKey: Movement along the demand curve (contraction): own-price change: movement up the existing curve.

items.stem: The demand for rice in Quentara is Qd = 360 − 6P. After a successful advertising campaign, demand becomes Qd = 410 − 6P. Calculate the change in quantity demanded at a price of $8.
items.answer: +50 units
items.markingKey: Before 312, after 362; change +50.

items.stem: The demand for bus journeys in Ostrelia is Qd = 360 − 10P. After a rise in incomes (normal good), demand becomes Qd = 400 − 10P. (a) Calculate the quantity demanded at $5 before and after the change. (b) State whether this is a shift or a movement along the demand curve and explain why. (c) Explain the cause using the conditions of demand.
items.answer: (a) 310 → 350 units. (b) A shift right: quantity demanded changes at every price, not because of the good’s own price. (c) The rise in incomes (normal good) changes a condition of demand.
items.markingKey: (a) both values [2] (b) shift and direction [1]; reason [1] (c) cause explained [1] [5]

items.stem: The government of Fendaria has asked its economic advisers for a report on this issue. With the help of diagrams, explain the difference between a movement along and a shift of a demand curve.
items.answer: Own price → extension/contraction; conditions of demand (income, related goods, tastes, population, expectations) → shift; diagrams showing both.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Own price → extension/contraction; conditions of demand (income, related goods, tastes, population, expectations) → shift; diagrams showing both. Level 3 (6–8): accurate knowledge with a clear, developed analytical chain and, where relevant, an accurate, labelled diagram that is used in the answer; Level 2 (3–5): some correct explanation but undeveloped or partly inaccurate; Level 1 (1–2): limited knowledge, mostly assertion [8]

items.stem: Which would shift the supply curve of rice to the right?
options: A rise in the price of rice
An increase in the wages of farm workers
items.answer: Improved irrigation that raises yields
items.markingKey: Lower costs/higher productivity raise supply.

items.stem: Farmers in Nordavia expect the price of their crop to rise next year. Explain why current supply may fall.
items.answer: Farmers hold back stocks to sell later at the higher price, so current supply shifts left.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: withhold stock; 1 mark: current supply falls [2]

items.stem: Lina makes the following statement: ‘A rise in the price of smartphones shifts the supply curve to the right.’ Identify what is wrong with this reasoning and give the correct explanation.
items.answer: A rise in the good’s own price causes an extension along the supply curve, not a shift.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies the error; 1 mark: correct explanation – A rise in the good’s own price causes an extension along the supply curve, not a shift. [2]

items.stem: A new technology reduces the cost of producing cement. What is the effect on the supply curve of cement?
options: Shift of the supply curve to the left
Shift of the supply curve to the right
items.answer: Shift of the supply curve to the right
items.markingKey: Shift of the supply curve to the right: lower unit costs raise supply at every price.

items.stem: The supply of solar panels is given by Qs = 20 + 5P, where Q is in thousands of units and P in dollars. Calculate the quantity supplied when the price is $15.
items.answer: 95 thousand

items.stem: The supply of textiles is given by Qs = 20 + 2P, where Q is in thousands of units and P in dollars. (a) Calculate the change in quantity supplied when the price changes from $8 to $20. (b) A new technology increases supply by 15 thousand units at every price. Write the new supply equation and calculate the quantity supplied at $20. (c) Distinguish between the two changes in (a) and (b).
items.answer: (a) 36 → 60: +24 thousand. (b) Qs = 35 + 2P; 75 thousand. (c) (a) is a movement along the supply curve (own price); (b) is a rightward shift (non-price factor).
items.markingKey: (a) [1] (b) equation [1]; quantity [1] (c) movement vs shift [2] [5]

items.stem: The government of Valdoria has asked its economic advisers for a report on this issue. Consider whether technological change is the most important cause of increases in supply in the long run.
items.answer: For: Lowers unit costs and raises productivity; major shifts in agriculture and electronics. Against: Factor prices, government taxes and subsidies, entry of firms and weather also shift supply; in the short run weather/costs dominate; depends on industry. Conclusion: a reasoned judgement on when the claim holds.
items.markingKey: Analysis (AO1/AO2, up to 8): Lowers unit costs and raises productivity; major shifts in agriculture and electronics. Evaluation (AO3, up to 4): Factor prices, government taxes and subsidies, entry of firms and weather also shift supply; in the short run weather/costs dominate; depends on industry. Top marks need balanced analysis of both sides and a justified conclusion that answers the question set, explaining what the outcome depends on [12]

items.stem: Why does a demand curve usually slope downwards from left to right?
options: Firms produce more at lower prices
Costs of production fall as output rises
At lower prices consumers can afford more and the good becomes better value relative to substitutes
Government sets lower prices for larger quantities
items.answer: At lower prices consumers can afford more and the good becomes better value relative to substitutes
items.markingKey: Income and substitution effects; diminishing marginal utility.

items.stem: During a class discussion Yusuf said: ‘Everyone who wants a good forms part of its demand.’ Explain what is wrong with this claim.
items.answer: Only effective demand counts: the desire must be backed by the ability and willingness to pay.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies the error; 1 mark: correct explanation – Only effective demand counts: the desire must be backed by the ability and willingness to pay. [2]

items.stem: In a revision note Diego wrote: ‘When the price of laptops falls, demand for laptops increases, so the demand curve shifts to the right.’ Identify what is wrong with this reasoning and give the correct explanation.
items.answer: A fall in the good’s own price causes an extension of demand: a movement along the existing demand curve, not a shift.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies the error; 1 mark: correct explanation – A fall in the good’s own price causes an extension of demand: a movement along the existing demand curve, not a shift. [2]

items.answer: Demand rises for normal goods but falls for inferior goods.

options: Shift of the demand curve to the left
Shift of the demand curve to the right
items.answer: Shift of the demand curve to the left
items.markingKey: Shift of the demand curve to the left: tastes and preferences have moved against the good.

items.stem: The demand for smartphones in Pelora is Qd = 240 − 5P. After a rise in incomes (normal good), demand becomes Qd = 290 − 5P. Calculate the change in quantity demanded at a price of $10.
items.answer: +50 units
items.markingKey: Before 190, after 240; change +50.

items.stem: The demand for gym memberships in Gorvania is Qd = 200 − 5P. After a successful advertising campaign, demand becomes Qd = 250 − 5P. (a) Calculate the quantity demanded at $12 before and after the change. (b) State whether this is a shift or a movement along the demand curve and explain why. (c) Explain the cause using the conditions of demand.
items.answer: (a) 140 → 190 units. (b) A shift right: quantity demanded changes at every price, not because of the good’s own price. (c) The successful advertising campaign changes a condition of demand.
items.markingKey: (a) both values [2] (b) shift and direction [1]; reason [1] (c) cause explained [1] [5]

items.stem: Extract: The price of coffee beans on world markets rose from $3.0 to $3.9 per kilogram after frosts damaged crops in major producing countries. In Fendaria, cafés raised the price of a cup of coffee, yet the number of cups sold in Riyadh still rose slightly because incomes grew by 5% and coffee became more fashionable among young people. Sales of tea fell. (a) Explain the effect of the frosts on the supply curve of coffee beans. (b) Explain why sales of tea fell. (c) Discuss whether the rise in coffee prices is likely to be permanent.
items.answer: (a) Shift to the left: fewer beans available at every price. (b) Changes in tastes towards coffee shifted demand for tea (a substitute) to the left. (c) Supply recovers after frosts (new crops), new producers enter; but climate change may cause repeated shocks; demand growth persists; judgement.
items.markingKey: (a) Credit: Shift to the left: fewer beans available at every price. [2] (b) Credit: Changes in tastes towards coffee shifted demand for tea (a substitute) to the left. [2] (c) Credit: Supply recovers after frosts (new crops), new producers enter; but climate change may cause repeated shocks; demand growth persists; judgement. [4]

items.stem: Why does a supply curve usually slope upwards?
options: Consumers buy more at higher prices
Higher prices make production more profitable and cover the higher costs of extra output
items.answer: Higher prices make production more profitable and cover the higher costs of extra output
items.markingKey: Profit incentive; rising marginal cost.

items.stem: During a class discussion Priya said: ‘A rise in the price of textiles shifts the supply curve to the right.’ Explain what is wrong with this claim.
items.answer: A rise in the good’s own price causes an extension along the supply curve, not a shift.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies the error; 1 mark: correct explanation – A rise in the good’s own price causes an extension along the supply curve, not a shift. [2]

items.stem: Farmers in Korvia expect the price of their crop to rise next year. Explain why current supply may fall.
items.answer: Farmers hold back stocks to sell later at the higher price, so current supply shifts left.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: withhold stock; 1 mark: current supply falls [2]

items.stem: The government gives producers of car tyres a subsidy. What is the effect on the supply curve of car tyres?
options: Shift of the supply curve to the left
Shift of the supply curve to the right
items.answer: Shift of the supply curve to the right
items.markingKey: Shift of the supply curve to the right: a subsidy lowers producers’ costs.

items.stem: The supply of laptops is given by Qs = −10 + 4P, where Q is in thousands of units and P in dollars. Calculate the quantity supplied when the price is $10.
items.answer: 30 thousand

items.stem: The supply of washing machines is given by Qs = 10 + 3P, where Q is in thousands of units and P in dollars. (a) Calculate the change in quantity supplied when the price changes from $10 to $20. (b) A new technology increases supply by 10 thousand units at every price. Write the new supply equation and calculate the quantity supplied at $20. (c) Distinguish between the two changes in (a) and (b).
items.answer: (a) 40 → 70: +30 thousand. (b) Qs = 20 + 3P; 80 thousand. (c) (a) is a movement along the supply curve (own price); (b) is a rightward shift (non-price factor).
items.markingKey: (a) [1] (b) equation [1]; quantity [1] (c) movement vs shift [2] [5]

items.stem: A policy institute in Dhaka has published a report on this issue for the government of Jovania. ‘Technological change is the most important cause of increases in supply in the long run.’ Evaluate this view.
items.answer: For: Lowers unit costs and raises productivity; major shifts in agriculture and electronics. Against: Factor prices, government taxes and subsidies, entry of firms and weather also shift supply; in the short run weather/costs dominate; depends on industry. Conclusion: a reasoned judgement on when the claim holds.
items.markingKey: Analysis (AO1/AO2, up to 8): Lowers unit costs and raises productivity; major shifts in agriculture and electronics. Evaluation (AO3, up to 4): Factor prices, government taxes and subsidies, entry of firms and weather also shift supply; in the short run weather/costs dominate; depends on industry. Top marks need balanced analysis of both sides and a justified conclusion that answers the question set, explaining what the outcome depends on [12]
